prompt.context: Your client, Croquet, is a domestic clothing brand that sells exclusively in its stores across the continental United States. Croquet is a premium brand with a high focus on customer service in its stores. It has recently experienced a downturn in sales, even though its collections have received positive press and are on trend. You have been brought on to help reverse the downward slide.
prompt.question: What is driving the downturn in Croquet's sales, and how would you recommend reversing it?

clarifying_info.q: How many stores does Croquet operate?
clarifying_info.a: Croquet operates 120 stores and the downturn has been experienced across all markets.

clarifying_info.q: Are there new competitors taking share?
clarifying_info.a: No new competitors have entered the market that are taking significant share.

clarifying_info.q: Are there any supply chain or quality issues?
clarifying_info.a: Croquet owns its own manufacturing facilities in Asia and has had no issues with quality or deliveries.
Croquet has not significantly changed its inventory strategy — price point, target demographic, and inventory mix have stayed the same.
Stores are staffed by management (salaried) and hourly staff. Croquet pays a competitive hourly wage but no commission.

exhibits.title: FY16 vs. FY17 Retail Metrics and Average Sales by Day
exhibits.shows: Two tables: (1) year-over-year retail metrics including Traffic, Conversion, Annual Sales, and DPLH for FY16 and FY17; (2) average sales by day of week for FY16 Actual, FY17 Plan, and FY17 Actual across Sunday through Saturday.

exhibits.title: FY16 and FY17 Average Labor Hours per Day Plan vs. Actual
exhibits.shows: A table showing average labor hours per day of week for FY16 Actual, FY17 Plan, and FY17 Actual across Sunday through Saturday.

framework: Focus on revenue drivers: traffic, conversion rate, and average transaction value
Examine whether the decline is concentrated in specific stores, regions, days of week, or customer segments
Investigate labor and staffing as a potential driver of conversion and service quality
Assess management incentive structures and how they influence operational decisions
Consider pricing, inventory, and in-store experience factors

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, calculate the number of transactions for FY16 and FY17. What is the percentage difference, and how does it compare to the percentage difference in sales?
questions.guidance: A strong candidate multiplies traffic by conversion to get transactions, notes the small decline in transactions (~2%) versus the much larger decline in sales (13%), and flags that the DPLH being roughly flat while sales fell means labor hours must be down.

math.setup: Transactions = Traffic x Conversion Rate; Sales decline = (FY17 - FY16) / FY16
steps: DPLH is up slightly ($17.39 vs $17.35); since sales are down and DPLH is up, labor hours must be down
math.answer: Transactions fell ~2% but sales fell ~13%, indicating a drop in average transaction value or a more severe problem beyond traffic/conversion. DPLH being flat implies labor hours declined.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, how do FY17 actual sales compare to FY17 plan by day of week? Where is the biggest miss?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify that early-week days (Sun–Fri) met or exceeded plan, but Saturday fell dramatically short: $29M actual vs. $56M planned versus $54M in FY16. The Saturday miss is the primary driver of the overall shortfall.

math.setup: Compare FY17 Actual to FY17 Plan and to FY16 Actual for each day
steps: Sunday: $26M actual vs $25M plan — over plan
Mon–Thu: $9.5M each vs $9M plan — slightly over
Saturday: $29M actual vs $56M plan and $54M FY16 — massive miss
math.answer: Saturday is the dominant problem: $27M below plan and $25M below prior year, accounting for the bulk of the $16M annual shortfall.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2, calculate total weekly labor hours for FY16 Actual, FY17 Plan, and FY17 Actual. What do you notice about the distribution of hours across the week?
questions.guidance: Candidate should sum the hours, note that planned hours are down from FY16, stores are meeting their plans, and critically that hours have been shifted away from Saturday (the highest-revenue day) toward earlier in the week.

math.setup: Sum labor hours across all 7 days for each scenario
steps: Saturday hours: FY16=38, FY17 Plan=33, FY17 Actual=27 — actual is 6 below even the reduced plan
Early-week (Mon–Wed) FY17 Actual exceeds plan while Saturday is 6 hours below plan
math.answer: Total hours are meeting plan (~115), but hours are being front-loaded to Sun–Wed and cut on Saturday. Saturday actual hours (27) are 11 below FY16 (38) and 6 below FY17 plan (33).

questions.prompt: What behaviors might explain why managers are cutting Saturday hours and front-loading early-week hours?
questions.guidance: After brainstorming, reveal that corporate incorporated weekly labor plans into managers' incentive bonuses. A strong candidate identifies the incentive misalignment: managers cut expensive Saturday hours (which cost more per hour in busy periods) to hit the weekly labor budget and earn their bonus, at the cost of peak-day revenue.

brainstorming.prompt: Why might store managers be front-loading labor hours to the beginning of the week and cutting hours on Saturdays?

categories.name: Workforce availability
ideas: Employees unavailable or unwilling to work weekends
High turnover of hourly staff making Saturday scheduling difficult
Employees calling in sick on weekends

categories.name: Management incentives
ideas: Corporate tied weekly labor-hour targets to manager bonus
Managers cut Saturday hours (highest-cost day) to meet weekly labor plan
Managers can set weekly schedules and adjust them to hit labor targets

categories.name: Operational decisions
ideas: Managers prioritize early-week tasks (receiving, restocking) over floor coverage
Lack of visibility into the revenue impact of cutting Saturday hours

recommendation: Remove weekly labor hours from management incentive bonus or replace with a sales/revenue-based metric to eliminate the incentive to cut peak-day staffing
Restructure scheduling to protect Saturday hours — shift labor from early week (Mon–Wed) back to Friday and Saturday to capture peak demand
Consider introducing commission or sales-based incentives for hourly associates to drive conversion and average transaction value
Evaluate a training program focused on customer service and upselling to improve conversion and basket size
Consider targeted promotions or events on Saturdays to further capitalize on peak traffic
risks: If labor costs rise without a proportional sales recovery, profitability may not improve
Commission structures can create undesirable associate behaviors (e.g., overselling, conflict over customers)
Scheduling changes require manager buy-in; cultural resistance may slow implementation
next_steps: Pilot revised scheduling and incentive structure in a subset of stores and measure conversion and sales lift
Analyze whether inventory levels on Saturdays are sufficient to meet demand
Assess whether the labor cost savings from the current plan are real or illusory given the revenue miss
